exercises.name: hello1
hello2
exercises.hint: `main` promises an int and has to keep the promise on every path. End it with `return 0;` — 0 is the exit code that means success.

exercises.name: variables1
exercises.hint: `let` binds a name once. A binding that is assigned again later has to be declared with `var`.

exercises.name: variables2
exercises.hint: The compiler counts only what BOTH branches of an if/else assign. Give the `if` an `else` branch that assigns `label` too — or initialize `label` where it is declared.

exercises.name: variables3
exercises.hint: `null` fixes no type on its own: the compiler cannot know which `?T` you mean. Annotate the binding: `let found: ?int = null;`.

exercises.name: numbers1
exercises.hint: `int` and `int64` are distinct types even though both are 64 bits wide. A VARIABLE never adapts; only a literal does. Cross with a cast: `let wide: int64 = n as int64;`.

exercises.name: numbers2
exercises.hint: An `int8` holds -128..127, so the literal 200 does not fit and the compiler refuses to adapt it. The value is a byte: `uint8` (0..255) is the type that holds it.

exercises.name: numbers3
exercises.hint: `float * int` is not defined — no operand is converted for you. Convert explicitly with `as`: `price * (count as float)`.

exercises.name: numbers4
exercises.hint: Integer arithmetic WRAPS at the width of the operands: 127i8 + 1 is -128, 0u8 - 1 is 255, and 300 as int8 keeps the low eight bits (44). Fill in the three expected values accordingly.

exercises.name: numbers5
exercises.hint: Integer division by zero is a PANIC (LYR-VM0002): the process ends with exit code 101 and nothing catches it. Test the divisor before dividing and print the message for the zero case instead.

exercises.name: strings1
exercises.hint: `+` joins two strings; it does not turn a number into text. Either interpolate — `f"Hello, {name}, you are {age}"` — or convert with `std.string.fromInt(age)`.

exercises.name: strings2
exercises.hint: A string cannot be indexed: finding code point i costs O(n), and an index loop would be quadratic. Walk it with `for (c in word)` and count the characters as you go — or use `word.length()` and `word.charAt(0)` from std.string.
exercises.expect:
L, y, r, i, c
5 characters

exercises.name: strings3
exercises.hint: The string METHODS (`trim`, `toUpper`, `split`, …) come with std.string. Import the module under an alias so the builtin type name is not shadowed: `import std.string as strings;` — the methods are then visible on every string.

exercises.name: strings4
exercises.hint: A format specifier follows the expression after a colon: `{pi:N2}` renders two decimals, `{n:D3}` pads an integer to three digits. And a literal brace is doubled: `{{`.

exercises.name: functions1
exercises.hint: Once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it needs one too — otherwise a call with fewer arguments could not tell which slot it left out. Move `name` in front of `greeting`.

exercises.name: functions2
exercises.hint: Overloads are told apart by what they TAKE, never by what they return: two `describe(int)` are a redeclaration. The second one wants a string — change its parameter type to `string`.

exercises.name: functions3
exercises.hint: A lambda's parameters take their types from the context — here there is none, because `let` infers from the lambda instead of the other way round. Annotate: `(n: int) => n * 3`.

exercises.name: functions4
exercises.hint: `params` collects the surplus arguments into an array, so it can only be the LAST parameter. Put `label` first and `values` last — and update the calls to match.

exercises.name: control1
exercises.hint: As an EXPRESSION, `if` must produce a value on both paths, so `else` is mandatory: `let bonus = if (score > 50) 10 else 0;`.

exercises.name: control2
exercises.hint: A condition must be a `bool`; an `int` is never 'truthy'. Compare explicitly: `if (remaining != 0)` or `while (remaining > 0)`.

exercises.name: control3
exercises.hint: `a..b` is a loop head, not a value: there is no range type to store one in. Write the bounds into the `for` directly: `for (n in 1..=limit)`.

exercises.name: control4
exercises.hint: `break` leaves the loop for good; `continue` skips just this iteration. Skipping the even numbers is a `continue`. The `break` belongs to the other condition.

exercises.name: control5
exercises.hint: A `while` body may run zero times, so nothing it assigns counts afterwards. A `do { … } while (…)` body runs at least once, and its assignments DO count. Turn the loop around — the first attempt must happen anyway.

exercises.name: arrays1
exercises.hint: Every element of an array literal has the same type. `3.0` is a float among ints — write it as `3`, or make every element a float.

exercises.name: arrays2
exercises.hint: Indices run from 0 to `length - 1`. `0..=xs.length` includes the length itself — the exclusive range `0..xs.length` is the one that fits an array.

exercises.name: tuples1
exercises.hint: `divide` returns a pair — two elements, so the pattern binds two names: `let (quotient, remainder) = divide(17, 5);`.

exercises.name: arrays3
exercises.hint: An array is a REFERENCE value: `let b = a` makes two names for one array, so writing through `b` is visible through `a`. Both reads therefore give 99. (A copy is `a + []`, if you need one.)

exercises.name: structs1
exercises.hint: The initializer names a field the struct does not have. `Point` has `x` and `y` — the second coordinate is `y`, not `z`.

exercises.name: structs2
exercises.hint: A method that writes to `this` has to say so: `mut fn deposit(…)`. Without `mut`, `this` is read-only inside the method.

exercises.name: structs3
exercises.hint: A struct is a VALUE: `var b = a;` copies it, and writing `b.x` leaves `a.x` alone. So `a.x` is still 1, and `b.x` is 99.

exercises.name: classes1
exercises.hint: A class is a REFERENCE: `let second = first;` makes two names for one object, and `second.value = 5` is visible through `first` as well. Both reads give 5.

exercises.name: classes2
exercises.hint: `record` receives a COPY of the struct and bumps the copy; the caller's `tracker` never changes. State that several calls share belongs in a `class` — change the one keyword.

exercises.name: enums1
exercises.hint: `Rectangle` carries two floats, `Circle` one. The call `Shape.Circle(3.0, 4.0)` hands two values to a one-value variant — the second shape is a rectangle.

exercises.name: enums2
exercises.hint: A variant declared with braces — `Triangle { a, b, c }` — is constructed with braces and field names: `Shape.Triangle { a = 3.0, b = 4.0, c = 5.0 }`. The tuple form belongs to variants declared with parentheses.

exercises.name: enums3
exercises.hint: `==` on an enum needs an `Equatable` conformance the type does not declare. The idiomatic test for a variant is `match`: `match (light) { Red => …, _ => … }`.

exercises.name: enums4
exercises.hint: `let a = Outcome.Ok(21);` gives the compiler nothing to infer `T` from. Write the type arguments on the enum: `Outcome<int>.Ok(21)` — or annotate the binding.

exercises.name: matching1
exercises.hint: The match names what is missing: `Blue`. Add an arm for it — or end with `_ =>` if the remaining variants share an answer.

exercises.name: matching2
exercises.hint: A guarded arm never counts toward exhaustiveness — the compiler cannot know the guard holds. Add an unguarded arm after it: `Circle(r) => …` for the small circles.

exercises.name: matching3
exercises.hint: The scrutinee is an `int`; the arms test strings. Match the number itself: `0 =>`, `1 | 2 | 3 =>`, `4..=9 =>`, then a binding or `_` for the rest.

exercises.name: matching4
exercises.hint: A block arm contributes no value: it has to `return` or `throw` on every path. Either end the block with `return …;` or make the arm an expression — `Weekend => 0,`.

exercises.name: matching5
exercises.hint: The scrutinee is a `?Shape`: an optional enum. Its `null` state is one more case, and the match must name it: add a `null => …` arm.

exercises.name: matching6
exercises.hint: A name binds once per pattern. `Point { x = a, y = a }` names `a` twice; bind the second field to another name — `Point { x = a, y = b }`.

exercises.name: optionals1
exercises.hint: `find` answers `?int`, and a `?int` cannot be added to. Decide what happens when it is absent: `let hit = find(…) ?? -1;` gives a plain `int` — or test `if (hit != null)` and use `hit` inside, where it is narrowed to `int`.

exercises.name: optionals2
exercises.hint: Only a LOCAL or a PARAMETER narrows — a field does not, because someone else might write it between the test and the read. Read the field into a local first: `let nick = p.nickname; if (nick != null) { … }`.
exercises.expect:
Ada is ada42
Grace has no nickname

exercises.name: optionals3
exercises.hint: `!` is a promise that the value is there, and the second lookup breaks it: the unwrap panics. Say what to print when a key is missing with `??`: `lookup("port") ?? "unset"`.

exercises.name: optionals4
exercises.hint: `??=` assigns only when the left side is `null` — that is the whole point of it. A plain `=` overwrites the nickname the user chose. Write `nick ??= "anonymous";`.

exercises.name: optionals5
exercises.hint: A `?int` compares against `null` and against nothing else; the value inside is reached by narrowing. Test `if (age != null && age >= 18)` — to the right of `&&`, `age` is already an `int`.
exercises.expect:
Ada: adult
Grace: age unknown
Lin: minor

exercises.name: optionals6
exercises.hint: An iterator answers `?T` and spends `null` on 'the end', so a `(?int)[]` cannot be walked by `for-in` (LYR-SEM0091). Walk the indices — `for (i in 0..slots.length)` — and read `slots[i]`; or use `std.iter.compact`.

exercises.name: interfaces1
exercises.hint: `Square` declares `:: [Drawable]` and has to provide every method the interface names. Add `fn draw(): string { return "square"; }` to it.

exercises.name: interfaces2
exercises.hint: An implementation must match the interface's declaration exactly — here `area(): float`. Return a float from `Square.area`: `this.side * this.side` with `side: float`.

exercises.name: interfaces3
exercises.hint: The `equals` method alone enables nothing; the CONFORMANCE does. Declare `struct Point :: [Equatable<Point>]` and import `Equatable` from std.core.

exercises.name: interfaces4
exercises.hint: `<` comes from `Ordered<T>` and its single method `compare(other: T): int` — negative, zero or positive. Declare the conformance and write `compare` over major, then minor.

exercises.name: interfaces5
exercises.hint: `+` is `Add<Rhs, Out>` from std.core with one method `add(other: Rhs): Out`. Declare `struct Money :: [Add<Money, Money>]` and give it `fn add(other: Money): Money`.

exercises.name: interfaces6
exercises.hint: Index syntax comes from `Indexable<T>` in std.collections: `fn get(index: int): T` and `mut fn set(index: int, value: T): void`. Declare the conformance on `Grid` and rename the methods to match.

exercises.name: interfaces7
exercises.hint: `greet` is abstract, so `Casual` would have to implement it. Give the interface method a BODY — a default — and `Casual` inherits it while `Formal` keeps its own.

exercises.name: generics1
exercises.hint: `largest` needs `<` on its elements, and only a constraint can promise that: `fn largest<T :: [Ordered<T>]>(items: T[]): T`. Import `Ordered` from std.core.

exercises.name: generics2
exercises.hint: `report` requires `Describable`, and `int` does not conform. Pass something that does — `report(Coin { })` — or give `int` the conformance with an `extend int :: [Describable]` block.

exercises.name: generics3
exercises.hint: `emptyOf()` has no argument that could tell the compiler what `T` is. Write the type argument at the call: `emptyOf<string>()`.

exercises.name: generics4
exercises.hint: A generic TYPE in a value position always takes its arguments explicitly: `Box<int> { value = 9 }`. They are never inferred from the field values.

exercises.name: extend1
extend2
exercises.hint: `Plain` has a `draw` method but never declares the conformance, so it is not a `Drawable`. Add it in the extend block: `extend Plain :: [Drawable] { … }` — an extend may declare interfaces, exactly like the type itself.

exercises.name: extend3
exercises.hint: `unit` is a static extension: it belongs to the type. Call `Point.unit()`, not `origin.unit()`.

exercises.name: errors1
exercises.hint: `parse` may throw, and `main` neither handles nor declares it. `main` cannot declare `throws`, so handle it: wrap the call in `try { … } catch (e: Exception) { … }` and print `e.message()`.

exercises.name: errors2
exercises.hint: Only a type that implements `Throwable` can be thrown. `Throwable` is built in and asks for one method, `message(): string` — declare `class NotFound :: [Throwable]` and add it.

exercises.name: errors3
exercises.hint: There is no `finally`; a `try` always has at least one `catch`. Cleanup that must run whichever way the block ends is `defer` — put `defer println("closed")` at the top of `process`, and give the `try` a `catch`.

exercises.name: errors4
exercises.hint: A typed catch covers exactly its type. `lookup` throws `NotFound`, not `Exception`, so `catch (e: Exception)` leaves it unhandled. Catch `NotFound` — or catch everything with `catch (e)`.

exercises.name: errors5
exercises.hint: A panic ABORTS: no `catch` sees it and no `defer` runs. An exception UNWINDS: the defers run and the catch answers. Replace the `panic(…)` with `throw Exception { text = "…" }` — `work` already declares `throws Exception`.

exercises.name: coroutines1
exercises.hint: A coroutine hands values out through `yield`, one per resume; its `return` carries nothing. Drop the `return n;` at the end (or make it a bare `return;`) — the caller already pulls every value with `resume`.

exercises.name: coroutines2
exercises.hint: `resume` on a finished coroutine panics. `co.next()` is the lenient pull: it answers `?T`, and `null` once the body has run to its end. Loop on `next()` and stop at `null`.

exercises.name: coroutines3
exercises.hint: The throwability is part of the coroutine's TYPE, and every pull of it is a throw site. Wrap the loop in `try { … } catch (e: Exception) { … }` and print `e.message()`.
exercises.expect:
step 1
step 2
stopped: the third step failed

exercises.name: modules1
exercises.hint: The fix is in geometry.lyr, not in the entry file: `area` is not exported. Only `pub` declarations cross the module boundary — mark `area` with `pub`.

exercises.name: modules2
exercises.hint: A module path is a file path under the directory of the entry file: `import shapes.circle` looks for `shapes/circle.lyr`. The file beside this exercise is `shapes/disc.lyr` — import `shapes.disc`.

exercises.name: modules3
exercises.hint: The fix is in config.lyr: a file must agree with the path it was loaded from. It is imported as `config`, so its header must say `module config;` — or have no header at all.

exercises.name: modules4
exercises.hint: A QUALIFIED import binds the last path segment: `import std.io.console;` makes `console.println` available, not `println`. Either write `console.println(…)` or import selectively: `import std.io.console { println };`.

exercises.name: modules5
exercises.hint: Module constants are initialized in DECLARATION ORDER, and an initializer may read only what stands before it. Move `VERSION` above `BANNER`.

exercises.name: attributes1
exercises.hint: A struct becomes usable as an attribute on functions by conforming to the marker `OnFunction` from std.core: `pub struct Command :: [OnFunction] { … }`. Conformance decides, not the name.

exercises.name: attributes2
exercises.hint: `until = "4.0"` promised removal at 4.0, and the toolchain is past that: the declaration itself is an error now. Keep the promise — delete `old` and call `renew` — or, if the date was wrong, move `until` into the future.

exercises.name: stdlib1
exercises.hint: `parseInt` answers `?int` — `null` is the whole truth about "x". Give the sum a fallback: `total += parseInt(part) ?? 0;`.

exercises.name: stdlib2
exercises.hint: A static member of a generic type needs the type arguments on the type: `List<string>.empty()`.

exercises.name: stdlib3
exercises.hint: `Map.get` answers `?V`, because the key may be absent. `getOr(key, fallback)` answers `V`: `counts.set(word, counts.getOr(word, 0) + 1);`.

exercises.name: stdlib4
exercises.hint: A `Set<T>` hashes its elements, so `T` must conform to `Hashable<T>` — which implies `Equatable<T>`. Declare `struct Point :: [Hashable<Point>]` with `fn equals(other: Point): bool` and `fn hash(): int` (for example `this.x * 31 + this.y`).

exercises.name: stdlib5
exercises.hint: The adapters and `sum` work on an `Iterator<T>`, and an array is not one. `over<int>(evens)` is the entrance that walks an array.

exercises.name: stdlib6
exercises.hint: `expect` panics on `null` — it is the `!` with a message, for values that must be there. `std.option.map` transforms a present value and leaves `null` alone; combine it with `??` for the fallback: `map(age, (n: int) => n + 1) ?? 0`.

exercises.name: stdlib7
exercises.hint: `parse` answers `?JsonValue` — `null` means the text is not JSON. Test `if (doc == null) { … }` first; after the early return `doc` is narrowed, and `doc.field("name")` works. The accessors answer `null` too, hence the `?.` and `??`.

exercises.name: stdlib8
exercises.hint: A READ answers `?T`: `text(path)` is `null` when the file cannot be read. Decide what an unreadable file means here — `text(path) ?? "missing"` — and the type is a plain `string`.

exercises.name: stdlib9
exercises.hint: The assertion is right and the function is wrong: `clamp(15, 0, 10)` must answer 10, and `clamp(-3, 0, 10)` must answer 0. Fix `clamp` — the assertions are the specification.

exercises.name: quiz1
exercises.hint: `Map.get` answers `?int`; adding to it is the optional-arithmetic error from chapter 12. `counts.getOr(word, 0) + 1` is the plain number you want.

exercises.name: quiz2
exercises.hint: The match in `show` does not cover `Triangle` — the compiler names it. Add an arm: `Triangle { a, b, c } => f"triangle {a}/{b}/{c}"`.
exercises.expect:
circle r=1.5
rectangle 2x3
triangle 3/4/5
total area: 19.07

exercises.name: quiz3
exercises.hint: `transfer` calls `withdraw`, which throws `InsufficientFunds`, and neither handles nor declares it. Declare it: `fn transfer(…): void throws InsufficientFunds` — `main` already catches.
exercises.expect:
alice: 70, bob: 130
transfer failed: alice has 70, needs 500

exercises.name: quiz4
exercises.hint: `for-in` accepts a range, an array, a string, an `Iterable<T>` or an `Iterator<T>`. Make `Stack<T>` conform to `Iterable<T>` from std.iter: `fn iter(): Iterator<T>` returning a small iterator class with `mut fn next(): ?T` that walks `items` from the top.
